tehching-hsieh__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.text: Tehching Hsieh binds his life to a rule and lets time pass bodily. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun, by contrast, examines digital media as systems that remain stable through repetition, habit and permanent updating. For both, repetition produces no return to the same moment: the next punch on Hsieh's time clock uses up lifetime; the next update reproduces a network under changed conditions. Hsieh makes this consumption visible on the body, whereas digital media largely conceal it behind interfaces. In each case the rule stabilises a space of possible operations within which updating must take place again and again. Performance and platform thus move surprisingly close together.
tehching-hsieh__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.question: What would become visible if digital repetition were perceived as consumed lifetime, as it is with Hsieh?

dan-graham__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.text: Dan Graham builds situations in which people observe themselves and others observing; mirrors, glass and video delay make the present spatially and temporally unstable. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun describes networks, habits and updates as the conditions of digital presence. With Graham, one's own observation returns as an image; in the network, past behaviour returns as profile, recommendation or expectation. Both turn the traces of earlier operations into conditions of the next. Graham, however, exhibits this process as a perceptible experimental set-up, whereas on platforms it runs largely at the level of infrastructure. What is called a profile there might appear here as a time-delayed mirror.
dan-graham__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.question: How does self-observation change when the mirror already calculates ahead?

louise-bourgeois__gregory-bateson.text: Louise Bourgeois builds rooms, bodily forms and objects in which the past can become present again. Gregory Bateson asks when a difference within a context makes a further difference. Bourgeois' recurring forms can therefore be read as differences whose meaning changes with their respective context. The Cells stabilise spatial arrangements, but the event of perception cannot be held fast within them. Bateson's concept of pattern explains how relationships remain recognisable across repetitions; Bourgeois shows how bodily different such a recurrence can be experienced. Memory would then be neither merely a stored state nor pure repetition, but a present reorganisation of differences.
louise-bourgeois__gregory-bateson.question: Where is a memory located if it only becomes a difference in being perceived anew?

sol-lewitt__niklas-luhmann.text: Sol LeWitt separates the rule of a work from its particular material execution. Niklas Luhmann correspondingly distinguishes between structures, which restrict possibilities, and operations, which can only ever take place in the present. A Wall Drawing can therefore remain the same even though its concrete realisation passes away and is executed anew in another place. The instruction spatialises possibilities; each execution actualises only one of them. Yet the concrete drawing is not simply contained in the rule; it has to be produced. The work thus exists strangely between a repeatable structure of decisions and an unrepeatable act of execution.
sol-lewitt__niklas-luhmann.question: What exactly remains identical when a work exists only by being produced anew again and again?

felix-gonzalez-torres__george-spencer-br.text: Felix Gonzalez-Torres lets works shrink, disappear and be replenished without their thereby ceasing to be the same works. George Spencer-Brown begins with a simpler operation: a boundary is drawn and thereby produces a marked and an unmarked side. With Gonzalez-Torres, the boundary of the work likewise seems precisely determined and at the same time materially mobile. A sweet can leave the installation, be eaten and disappear, while the identity of the work persists. The form, then, does not necessarily stabilise itself through the identity of its components. Spencer-Brown's boundary prompts the question of where the relevant distinction actually runs here: between work and non-work, rule and material, presence and absence?
felix-gonzalez-torres__george-spencer-br.question: How much can a form lose and still remain the same?

christian-marclay__gregory-bateson.text: Christian Marclay's The Clock assembles thousands of filmic depictions of clock times so that they coincide with the actual time of the audience. Gregory Bateson understands information not as a thing but as a difference that makes a difference within a context. A clock time shown on screen is therefore at first only a difference; only its relation to the viewer's present time makes it an event. Marclay spatialises enormous quantities of past film time in an assembled archive and temporalises this archive again through its screening. The same excerpt thereby acquires a different operative meaning at 14:37 than outside this synchronisation. Past and present do not become identical, but are for a moment related to one another.
christian-marclay__gregory-bateson.question: What exactly do we perceive when a depicted time suddenly designates our own time?

donald-judd__michel-serres.text: Donald Judd arranges bodies and intervals with great metrical precision. Michel Serres, by contrast, also thinks space through paths, neighbourhoods and transitions. With Judd, the distance between two objects remains measurably the same, while their relationship changes as one walks. What stands side by side becomes a sequence of nearness and distance only through the path of the body.
donald-judd__michel-serres.question: Is nearness a question of distance or of the path?

bruce-nauman__jacques-derrida.text: Bruce Nauman repeats movements, words, gestures and video sequences until their apparent identity becomes unstable. Jacques Derrida describes iterability precisely in that something must be repeatable in order to function as a sign, yet inscribes itself with each repetition in a new context. Nauman's loops make this shift bodily perceptible. The technical recording can return identically; the perceiving body does not. What was stabilised spatially or in a medium therefore produces a sequence of different presents. With Nauman, Derrida's trace almost acquires a body.
bruce-nauman__jacques-derrida.question: Where does the repetition lie if only the recording stays the same?

james-turrell__hannah-arendt.text: James Turrell builds spaces in which light does not merely make something visible but in which seeing itself becomes conspicuous. Hannah Arendt describes the public as a space of appearance that arises when people become visible and audible to one another. Turrell produces this space technically and architecturally; Arendt understands it as the relational condition of acting together. Neither, then, treats appearing as a self-evident property of existing things. Something can appear only if conditions exist under which it can appear. The difference is decisive: with Turrell this concerns, first of all, perception; with Arendt, a world brought forth in common.
james-turrell__hannah-arendt.question: What happens to a common world when even the conditions of its appearing are unequally distributed?

william-kentridge__donna-haraway.text: William Kentridge draws, erases and draws again, while earlier states remain on the paper as smeared traces. Donna Haraway turns against the view from nowhere and insists that knowledge arises from concrete, situated positions. Kentridge's sheet likewise no longer possesses an innocent initial state: each new drawing arises on the material consequences of earlier decisions. The place from which work continues already carries its history with it. Haraway's situatedness here acquires a temporal dimension; position would be not only a where but also an after-what. At the same time, the animation makes this irreversible history technically replayable.
william-kentridge__donna-haraway.question: Can a place be determined without taking its history into account?

agnes-martin__elena-esposito.text: Agnes Martin stabilises seeing through grids, repetition and minimal deviation. Elena Esposito examines how communication deals with a future that does not yet exist but becomes effective in the present through expectations, probabilities and forecasts. Martin's grid seems at first to do the opposite: it reduces possibilities to an almost unchanging order. Yet it is precisely this stability that makes the smallest shifts in perception noticeable. With Esposito, models stabilise expectations without being able to fix the coming present. In both cases an order creates the conditions for something to appear that is not yet contained within it.
agnes-martin__elena-esposito.question: How much order does the unforeseeable need in order to appear as change at all?

agnes-martin__judith-butler.text: Agnes Martin repeats lines and grids; Judith Butler examines how norms become effective through repetition. In both cases repetition produces stability without ever simply bringing forth the same thing. For Butler, a norm can persist only by being enacted again and again, and precisely therein lies the possibility of its displacement. Martin's grid seems unchanging, yet it is perceived anew with every glance and is materially different in every execution. The decisive difference lies in the site of this repetition: with Butler it organises social legibility, with Martin a situation of perception.
agnes-martin__judith-butler.question: When does repetition stabilise an order, and when does it begin to tip precisely through its repetition?

hanne-darboven__niklas-luhmann.text: Hanne Darboven inscribes time in numbers, dates, series and sheets. Niklas Luhmann, by contrast, does not describe time as something that could be stored anywhere: operations happen and vanish; only present operations can connect to past ones. Darboven's vast arrangements seem to preserve past time spatially. Yet the archive itself becomes present only when someone reads, counts, looks or turns the page. The place on the sheet can be found again; the moment of its making cannot. Storage and recurrence thus come apart.
hanne-darboven__niklas-luhmann.question: What do we actually preserve when we say that a past has been stored?

eva-hesse__michel-foucault.text: Eva Hesse produces serial forms whose materials can age, sag, discolour and decay. Michel Foucault examines orders that distribute bodies, things and statements to particular places and thereby make them visible and comparable. Hesse's works seem at first to offer such orders themselves: series, repetitions, intervals. Yet their material does not reliably keep to the order it was given. What appears as a spatial system begins to develop a history of its own. Foucault makes visible how orders shape bodies; Hesse prompts the question of what happens when material answers its order with ageing, gravity and deformation.
eva-hesse__michel-foucault.question: How long does a body belong to an order whose form it no longer keeps?

marina-abramovic__susan-leigh-star.text: Marina Abramović frequently reduces performances to a few rules, a particular place and a present body. Susan Leigh Star examines infrastructures and boundary objects that make collaboration possible even though the participants understand them differently. A performance, too, requires such an infrastructure: space, institution, schedule, audience, rules and documentation must come together before the seemingly immediate encounter can take place. But whereas infrastructure works especially well when it becomes invisible, Abramović makes presence demonstratively visible. The body at the centre can thereby conceal the many conditions that organise its presence in the first place.
marina-abramovic__susan-leigh-star.question: What do we see when we look at the infrastructure of the performance?

rebecca-horn__claude-shannon.text: Rebecca Horn extends bodies with feathers, rods, masks and machines, thereby altering reach, distance and touch. Claude Shannon, by contrast, abstracts communication into message, channel, signal and statistical selection. The body almost entirely disappears from his model. Horn could at first be read as a reversal of this abstraction: with her, the channel itself becomes bodily. An extension of the arm does not simply transmit a movement from A to B; it changes what the body can reach and perceive. The material form of the channel becomes part of the event.
rebecca-horn__claude-shannon.question: What remains of the concept of transmission when the channel changes what can be perceived at all?

mona-hatoum__elena-esposito.text: Mona Hatoum takes familiar things and spaces and alters their scale, materials or relations so that familiarity turns into insecurity. Elena Esposito examines how present communication generates expectations about an unknown future. Both begin with something known: a household object, a body of data, a regularity observed so far. Hatoum alters the situation so that the known suddenly no longer offers reliable orientation. Forecasts do almost the opposite: they use the known to make uncertainty manageable again. Here two opposing movements stand side by side. Hatoum produces insecurity from familiar forms. Esposito asks how expectations arise out of uncertainty.
mona-hatoum__elena-esposito.question: What do we perceive when the forms with which we reduce uncertainty themselves become uncertain?

on-kawara__michel-foucault.text: On Kawara paints a date and makes a past day retrievable as an unambiguously designated place. Michel Foucault examines archives as orders that do not simply store everything past but determine what can become findable, distinguishable and assignable as a statement. Kawara's date paintings work like elementary archives: a day is given an address. At the same time, almost everything that happened on that day disappears. It is precisely the utmost precision of the date that produces an enormous blank. The archive thus preserves not the past itself but an order under which something past can be addressed again.
on-kawara__michel-foucault.question: How much must be forgotten for a past moment to receive an unambiguous address?

donald-judd__henri-bergson.text: Donald Judd organises bodies, intervals and repetitions with great spatial precision. Henri Bergson distrusts precisely the operation by which time is treated like a series of points lying side by side. For him, duration is not a sequence of interchangeable places but qualitative change, in which earlier moments continue to work within later ones. Judd's serial objects seem at first to stand on the other side: one beside the other, measurably separate. Yet a viewer can never perceive this series from all positions at once. He must move, remember and carry previous views into the next.
donald-judd__henri-bergson.question: Does a wholly spatial order inevitably give rise to a time as soon as someone begins to perceive it?

william-kentridge__claude-shannon.text: William Kentridge draws, erases and draws on; Claude Shannon describes information as a selection from a defined space of possible messages. For Shannon, it must be clear which alternatives are possible before information content can be calculated at all. Kentridge's sheet seems precisely not to hold such a space of possibilities in readiness. Each drawing alters the surface on which the next will arise; even erasing does not restore the earlier state. The possibilities of the next stroke thus depend on an irreversible history of the material. What appears mathematically as a selection among possibilities becomes, with Kentridge, a selection that alters its own space of possibilities.
william-kentridge__claude-shannon.question: How can a possibility be determined when every decision changes what is still possible afterwards?

agnes-martin__n-katherine-hayles.text: Agnes Martin produces pictures from lines, intervals and repetitions whose differences often emerge only on close perception. N. Katherine Hayles examines what is lost when information is thought independently of its material carrier. Martin's grid could easily be described as an abstract pattern and stored as a sequence of intervals or coordinates. But that would not yet explain what happens when pencil, paint, canvas, light and a perceiving body come together. It is precisely the small irregularities of her lines that show that a structure is not identical with its material embodiment. Hayles thus shifts the question from pattern to its embodiment, Martin from the grid to its perception.
agnes-martin__n-katherine-hayles.question: What is lost when a perceived form can be fully described as information?

mona-hatoum__claude-shannon.text: Mona Hatoum alters familiar objects and spatial situations so that orientation can turn into irritation. Claude Shannon, by contrast, must determine for his theory of information precisely which possible signals can be distinguished and transmitted. A channel works only if differences can be determined within a defined system. Hatoum's artistic operation takes hold at a different point: it is not necessarily the signal that changes but the situation within which something is perceived as familiar, dangerous, near or far. Shannon can measure that a difference has been transmitted; that does not yet determine what this difference means for a body.
mona-hatoum__claude-shannon.question: Where does meaning begin when a technically determinable difference suddenly alters a bodily situation?

robert-smithson__hannah-arendt.text: Robert Smithson shifts material between site and exhibition and, with Site and Nonsite, makes the difference between a place and its representation itself the subject; at the same time he is preoccupied with displacement and entropy. Hannah Arendt is interested in how a common world comes into being in which people and things appear and relationships can gain duration. With Smithson, however, a place precisely cannot be transferred completely into this common space: the stone in the museum is at the site of its exhibition and at the same time points to another place. The world then consists not simply of things in their places but also of relations between present and absent places. Through Smithson, Arendt's space of appearance acquires, as it were, a geological disturbance.
robert-smithson__hannah-arendt.question: Can something be present in common whose decisive place remains absent?

roman-opalka__lucy-suchman.text: Roman Opalka's sequence of numbers has the simplest conceivable plan: after the next number comes the next. Lucy Suchman, however, distinguishes between plans and situated action: an order can orient action without anticipating its concrete execution. With Opalka, the symbolic continuation can be determined exactly, but the execution is bound to hand, attention, fatigue and lifetime. The plan knows which number should follow; it does not know under what bodily conditions it will be painted. The predictability of the series and the openness of the event thus come apart.
roman-opalka__lucy-suchman.question: How much future can a plan contain if its execution only becomes real in a situation?

sol-lewitt__george-spencer-brown.text: George Spencer-Brown begins with a distinction: a boundary is drawn, and with it two sides arise. Sol LeWitt frequently also begins with a formal stipulation, an instruction, a grid, particular lines or rules of combination. What becomes decisive is what happens to this stipulation in execution. LeWitt himself stresses that different executors understand the same instruction differently and that even the same person does not realise the same plan identically twice; plan and execution nonetheless remain related to one another. Spencer-Brown makes the operation of distinction formally determinable, whereas LeWitt lets us observe what happens to a determination as soon as it has to be executed. The rule stabilises a space of possibilities, but it does not fully contain its concrete actualisation.
sol-lewitt__george-spencer-brown.question: Where does the form lie: in the rule or in its execution?

agnes-martin__gilles-deleuze.text: Agnes Martin repeats grids, lines and intervals without making identical pictures out of them. Gilles Deleuze sets repetition against the same at exactly this point: what recurs returns under changed conditions. Martin's works test this thought in a surprisingly direct way. The grid produces a strong identity of order, while material, the movement of the hand, light and perception bring forth differences. Without the recognisable order, however, these differences would hardly be experienceable as differences of the same thing. Martin thus leaves open whether difference precedes repetition or only becomes visible through it.
agnes-martin__gilles-deleuze.question: How much sameness does a difference need in order to be perceived as a difference?

hanne-darboven__donna-haraway.text: Hanne Darboven translates calendar time into numbers, writing, series and vast spatial arrangements. Donna Haraway insists that knowledge never comes from nowhere but remains bound to bodies, positions and concrete situations. Darboven's notations seem at first to detach time precisely from such situations: a date is given an abstract, retrievable place. Yet each sheet was written at a particular place and moment and is read anew by a particular body. The universal order of the calendar and the situated act do not coincide.
hanne-darboven__donna-haraway.question: What changes when a date also has a place of writing?

hanne-darboven__gilles-deleuze.text: Hanne Darboven repeats numbers, dates and operations of writing over decades. Gilles Deleuze would ask precisely in such repetition about the production of difference. Darboven's procedure is strict enough for deviations not to appear as mere arbitrariness. Each new entry belongs to the same operation and yet occupies a place that no other entry can occupy. The work thus makes difference visible not through spectacular change but through almost compulsive recurrence. The more similar the operation, the more clearly it emerges that no moment returns.
hanne-darboven__gilles-deleuze.question: Does repetition need a rule in order to produce difference at all?

hanne-darboven__lucy-suchman.text: Hanne Darboven organises her work through systems, calculations and recurring procedures. Lucy Suchman criticises the idea that a plan could already contain how an action will actually unfold. A plan provides resources for a situation; someone must first act in that situation. Darboven's works bring this difference onto paper: the rule can persist, but every page must actually be written. Between system and sheet lie time, labour and a body.
hanne-darboven__lucy-suchman.question: What does the execution of a rule add that cannot be present in the rule itself?

hanne-darboven__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.text: Hanne Darboven produces archives of her own operations through continued writing. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun examines digital cultures in which systems are at once changed and stabilised through updates and habits. Both combine continuation with repetition, but under almost opposite material conditions. Darboven's past operations remain visible as sheets; digital systems frequently overwrite earlier states precisely by updating themselves. The new can thus become the technique by which continuity is produced.
hanne-darboven__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.question: How do systems remember that constantly renew themselves?

eva-hesse__donna-haraway.text: Eva Hesse's works can be described formally, but their materials prevent a completely detached gaze. Donna Haraway understands knowledge as situated and thus bound to concrete conditions of observing. Latex, fibreglass, gravity and ageing are, with Hesse, not incidentals that could be factored out of the description. They help change what can be recognised of the form at all.
eva-hesse__donna-haraway.question: What does material change about our standpoint?

eva-hesse__gilbert-simondon.text: Eva Hesse's sculptures often look less like completed bodies than like provisionally stabilised material states. Gilbert Simondon likewise understands individuals not as finished unities but as results of continued individuation. This proximity must not, however, obscure the fact that Hesse's work has to remain identifiable as this work even when its material ages. The process thus meets a limit that makes Simondon's thinking of process particularly interesting: museums have to decide which changes still belong to the history of a work and which endanger its identity.
eva-hesse__gilbert-simondon.question: When is change the continuation of a form, and when does something else come into being?

eva-hesse__heinz-von-foerster.text: Eva Hesse repeats forms without eliminating the differences of their material execution. Heinz von Foerster examines how recursive processes can bring forth stable eigenforms. Hesse's series seem to offer such stability and undermine it at the same time. A form recurs, but material, position and perception prevent complete identity. Stability would then not be immutability but something that is recognised despite change.
eva-hesse__heinz-von-foerster.question: How much change can a form absorb and still recur as the same?

eva-hesse__n-katherine-hayles.text: N. Katherine Hayles criticises the idea that information could exist independently of its embodiment. Eva Hesse's works push this question into the material: a form in latex is not simply the same information in a different substance. Ageing, elasticity, transparency and gravity belong to what is perceived. One could measure Hesse's form digitally with exactness and still not store what happens to it over decades. Here the difference between describable structure and material eigentime shows itself.
eva-hesse__n-katherine-hayles.question: Which properties of a work can change carrier, and which disappear precisely in that change?

louise-bourgeois__george-spencer-brown.text: George Spencer-Brown begins with a boundary that divides a form into two sides. Louise Bourgeois, with her Cells, builds spaces whose boundaries can at once separate, protect, enclose and let the gaze pass through. With Spencer-Brown, the boundary is a formal precondition of distinction; with Bourgeois, it is experienced bodily. One stands before it, walks around it, looks in and remains outside. The marked and the unmarked side thereby acquire position, material and duration.
louise-bourgeois__george-spencer-brown.question: What happens to a distinction when its boundary itself has to be perceived?

louise-bourgeois__heinz-von-foerster.text: Louise Bourgeois returns over decades to forms, memories and conflicts without simply reproducing them. Heinz von Foerster describes recursion as an operation whose results can in turn become conditions of further operations. In this sense Bourgeois' recurrence could be understood less as a cycle than as recursive change. An earlier work or a memory is not retrieved but observed anew from a later present. The recurrence thereby also changes what appears as past.
louise-bourgeois__heinz-von-foerster.question: Can one return to something without at the same time changing that to which one returns?

louise-bourgeois__jacques-derrida.text: Louise Bourgeois often makes absence present through spaces, objects and bodily forms. Jacques Derrida's concept of the trace likewise designates no simple presence of the past: something is effective in the present precisely because what it points to is not fully present. Bourgeois gives this paradoxical structure material, weight and space. A garment, a bed or a locked cell can address something without bringing it back. Yet the perceived object is itself fully present.
louise-bourgeois__jacques-derrida.question: Can an absence be perceived, or do we only ever perceive something that designates it in the present?

marina-abramovic__gregory-bateson.text: Marina Abramović often alters a few conditions of a situation and observes what arises from this between body, audience and surroundings. Gregory Bateson understands information relationally: a difference becomes relevant only where it makes a further difference within a context. A minimal movement in a performance can therefore become more significant than a large change outside its rules. The situation helps decide which difference becomes noticeable at all. Abramović, however, adds a vulnerable body to Bateson's abstract relation.
marina-abramovic__gregory-bateson.question: When does a bodily change become information for another body?

marina-abramovic__judith-butler.text: Marina Abramović explicitly calls her works performances. Judith Butler, however, means something else by performativity: actions become socially legible because they connect to already existing norms. Abramović can determine the rules, duration and risk of a situation, but she cannot determine from scratch how her body is read within it. The performance is singular; its social legibility has a longer history.
marina-abramovic__judith-butler.question: What about a performance is legible beforehand?

marina-abramovic__karen-barad.text: Marina Abramović can reduce a situation to the point where body, objects, space and audience become unusually dependent on one another. Karen Barad disputes that observer and observed always already precede such situations as fully separate entities. An apparatus first brings forth certain boundaries and determinabilities. Abramović seems to supply an ideal example of this and at the same time a problem: her body remains vulnerable even if its meaning arises relationally. A cut can bring forth roles, but it cannot arbitrarily undo what has happened bodily.
marina-abramovic__karen-barad.question: Which boundaries arise only in the situation?

marina-abramovic__michel-serres.text: Marina Abramović uses the body not only as a depicted motif but as the medium of a situation with the audience. Michel Serres is interested in the fact that transmission never simply passes from one point to another: channels contain noise, detours and mediations. A performance, by contrast, seems to reduce mediation as far as possible; body and audience share place and time. Yet precisely this apparent immediacy needs space, rules, attention and bodily limits. Presence, too, has a channel.
marina-abramovic__michel-serres.question: What does immediate encounter mean if even presence needs conditions for its transmission?

marina-abramovic__henri-bergson.text: Henri Bergson distinguishes lived duration from a time that is broken down into measurable units and lined up side by side like places. Marina Abramović often works with fixed periods, repetition and bodily endurance. A performance can be described in hours, days or rules; but that does not capture how this time passes for body and audience. It is precisely the measurable framing that makes a second time noticeable: fatigue, expectation, boredom, concentration and change possess no uniform units. The spatialisation of time stabilises the experimental set-up, whereas its temporalisation takes place only in the irreversible act.
marina-abramovic__henri-bergson.question: What does a statement of duration measure, and what begins only where the measured time has to be lived through?

rebecca-horn__donna-haraway.text: Rebecca Horn joins bodies to feathers, rods, masks and machines. Donna Haraway's cyborg disturbs precisely the clear boundary between organism and technology. Horn's extensions do not simply illustrate this figure. They show bodily that reach, touch and action belong neither to the body alone nor to the apparatus alone.
rebecca-horn__donna-haraway.question: When does a technical extension become part of the body?

rebecca-horn__heinz-von-foerster.text: Heinz von Foerster makes the observer a component of observing. Rebecca Horn adds a changeable body to this abstract figure. Her apparatuses intervene in the conditions under which distance, movement and touch become possible. What changes is thus not merely the observed but the apparatus of observing itself. The observer cannot simply leave her own position; she can, however, rebuild its conditions.
rebecca-horn__heinz-von-foerster.question: Can one observe differently without thereby also becoming a different observer?

rebecca-horn__michel-serres.text: With Rebecca Horn, connections arise through extensions, machines, feathers, rods and moving bodies. Michel Serres is interested in passages, but equally in the noise and the change that accompany every passage. A prosthesis seems at first to bridge a distance. At the same time it produces a new distance: touch now takes place through something that steps between body and world. Connection and separation arise in the same operation.
rebecca-horn__michel-serres.question: Does an extension bring us closer to something, or does it produce a new form of the in-between?

mona-hatoum__n-katherine-hayles.text: N. Katherine Hayles criticises the idea that information could be detached from its material embodiment without something decisive being lost. Mona Hatoum makes familiar forms lose their self-evidence precisely through material, scale and spatial arrangement. An object can remain unambiguously recognisable as a form and yet become something entirely different for a body. Its geometry could be stored and transmitted; weight, temperature, resistance, nearness and possible danger arise only in a concrete embodiment. Hatoum thereby makes visible that the same describable structure can bring forth different situations of perception.
mona-hatoum__n-katherine-hayles.question: What remains of a form when its material becomes interchangeable?

mona-hatoum__hannah-arendt.text: Hannah Arendt describes a common world as something that at once connects people and separates them from one another, comparable to a table around which different positions are gathered. Mona Hatoum repeatedly transforms precisely familiar things and spatial orders into precarious situations. The common object then guarantees no common experience. People can stand before the same thing and yet be affected by it in completely different ways. Spatial commonality and shared world come apart.
mona-hatoum__hannah-arendt.question: What makes a space common when the people in it cannot appear under the same conditions?

mona-hatoum__judith-butler.text: Judith Butler examines how bodies become recognisable and legible as particular bodies within social norms. Mona Hatoum often tips familiar orders so that an object or space loses its accustomed legibility. This irritation concerns not only meaning but the body that has to relate to it. Something can look familiar and yet demand a different movement, distance or caution. Perception and social legibility thereby come apart.
mona-hatoum__judith-butler.question: What happens to a norm when the body has to act differently?

doris-salcedo__gilbert-simondon.text: Doris Salcedo works with objects and architectural interventions in which past violence remains present without simply being depicted. Gilbert Simondon understands forms not as final states but as provisional resolutions of tensions. Salcedo's works, by contrast, seem precisely to stabilise tensions that have found no resolution. Furniture, walls or fissures hold fast something that cannot be concluded. Form would here be less a resolution than continued material unrest.
doris-salcedo__gilbert-simondon.question: Can a form stabilise something precisely by preventing a tension from disappearing?

doris-salcedo__gregory-bateson.text: Gregory Bateson's famous definition of information demands a difference that makes a further difference. Doris Salcedo often works with absences whose effect consists precisely in the fact that something is no longer there. A blank can therefore make a difference even though it is not itself a present object. This works, however, only within a context in which the absence becomes noticeable at all. The context makes what is missing effective.
doris-salcedo__gregory-bateson.question: Can absence be information?

doris-salcedo__henri-bergson.text: Henri Bergson understands the past not as a collection of filed-away points in time but as something that continues to work within present duration. Doris Salcedo gives past losses material places in the present. Her works, however, do not make the past present again, as if it could be retrieved. Rather, an object carries a difference that time has not cancelled. Bergson's duration and Salcedo's material memory thus meet at a difficult boundary between continued effect and representation.
doris-salcedo__henri-bergson.question: How can the past be effective in the present without becoming present again?

doris-salcedo__niklas-luhmann.text: Niklas Luhmann treats the past as a construction available in the present: what has happened cannot return, but can only be remembered and designated through present operations. Doris Salcedo confronts this formal severity with material, body and loss. A work cannot repeat past violence and cannot bring back the lost person. But it can establish present conditions under which the absence receives attention anew. Communication does not take over the past event; it organises a new present around it.
doris-salcedo__niklas-luhmann.question: What exactly recurs when the event itself remains unrepeatable?

on-kawara__gilles-deleuze.text: On Kawara repeats the same elementary operation over decades: painting a date, on the day designated, according to strict rules; if the painting is not finished by midnight, it is destroyed. Gilles Deleuze separates repetition from the mere occurrence of the same. Kawara seems to test this distinction almost experimentally. The rule remains stable, while each execution designates a day that can never occur again. It is precisely the extreme similarity of the paintings that makes their temporal non-identity visible.
on-kawara__gilles-deleuze.question: Is it the repetition of the form that lets us recognise that the moment never repeats itself?

on-kawara__jacques-derrida.text: On Kawara's date paintings are radically unambiguous: each designates exactly the day on which it was made and must be completed within that day. Jacques Derrida, by contrast, draws attention to the fact that a sign can function precisely because it survives its original moment of origin and becomes legible again in other contexts. Kawara's date enacts exactly this paradox. 25 SEP. 2026 could designate a unique day and at the same time be read again decades later. The moment passes; its designation becomes repeatable.
on-kawara__jacques-derrida.question: What remains of a moment when only its sign lives on?

on-kawara__susan-leigh-star.text: On Kawara makes days addressable: date, format and rules transform unique lifetime into an ordered series. The Today paintings follow fixed formats and rules of production, while each individual day remains unrepeatable. Susan Leigh Star examines classifications and infrastructures that make heterogeneous realities comparable and coordinable. The calendar is one such powerful infrastructure: billions of different experiences can be filed under the same date position. Kawara uses this order without claiming that it contains the day in question.
on-kawara__susan-leigh-star.question: How much difference must a classification ignore for different events to be able to share the same place at all?

on-kawara__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.text: On Kawara binds each date painting to a single day and a strict rule of its making. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun examines digital media that produce the impression of a continuous present through permanent updating. Both combine actuality with repetition, but in opposite ways. With Kawara, each day is concluded and becomes irretrievably past; in the digital update, the past is continuously overwritten so that something can appear as present. The one procedure collects concluded presents; the other produces the present through renewal.
on-kawara__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.question: What becomes of the past when the present only ever appears as the next update?

tehching-hsieh__gilbert-simondon.text: Tehching Hsieh subjects his everyday life to a single rule over long periods. Gilbert Simondon understands individuals not as finished unities but as provisional results of continued individuation. Hsieh's performances place this processual character under unusually rigid conditions. The rule remains the same, while the body that executes it changes with every hour. What is stable, then, is precisely not the individual but the arrangement within which its change takes place.
tehching-hsieh__gilbert-simondon.question: What becomes visible through a rule that stays the same for longer than the body that follows it?

tehching-hsieh__jacques-derrida.text: Tehching Hsieh repeats actions under rules whose meaning arises precisely from their continued execution. Jacques Derrida describes repeatability as the condition for signs and actions to be able to function beyond their original context. With Hsieh, this repeatability meets lifetime: the next execution can be formally the same, but can no longer take place in the same moment or with the same body. Repetition requires a recognisable form and at the same time produces the trace of its passing.
tehching-hsieh__jacques-derrida.question: What does „the same once more“ mean when the once-more has already changed the conditions?

tehching-hsieh__karen-barad.text: Karen Barad directs attention to apparatuses that are not simply neutral environments but help determine which differences can be determined at all. For his performances, Tehching Hsieh builds downright radical apparatuses out of rule, clock, space and body. The time clock does not simply measure an already existing performance; it belongs to the conditions under which this performance can come into being. Yet the body does not remain arbitrarily definable by the experimental set-up: fatigue, ageing and vulnerability have consequences of their own.
tehching-hsieh__karen-barad.question: Which differences does an experimental set-up produce, and which differences does the body itself bring into it?

donald-judd__claude-shannon.text: Donald Judd arranges clearly distinguishable bodies and intervals; Claude Shannon requires clearly distinguishable possibilities in order to determine information mathematically. For both, difference seems at first to be a question of precise positions. Yet Judd's objects are not perceived as an abstract state space: a body moves past them, distances change, views disappear. Shannon gains calculability by removing precisely this concrete perception from his problem.
donald-judd__claude-shannon.question: What is added to a determinable difference as soon as it has to be perceived by someone?

donald-judd__gilbert-simondon.text: Donald Judd's works emphasise particular forms, materials, dimensions and relations in space. Gilbert Simondon, by contrast, is interested in how individuals emerge from processes and can never be fully separated from their coming into being. Judd's industrially fabricated objects at first look like counter-arguments: precisely determined and complete. Yet they too exist only through material, fabrication, architecture, light and the particular situation of perception. The determinate form and the processes of its production can be distinguished, but not fully detached from one another.
donald-judd__gilbert-simondon.question: When does a process become a thing, and what has to become invisible in the process?

donald-judd__karen-barad.text: Karen Barad asks how material arrangements bring forth the boundaries of what can be determined in a situation. Donald Judd builds arrangements in which object, interval, wall, floor and the viewer's position are related to one another with unusual precision. The object alone is therefore not enough to determine what is perceived. At the same time, Judd's concrete materiality resists the idea that the boundaries of the situation are merely effects of its observation. Steel remains steel; distance remains something to be crossed bodily.
donald-judd__karen-barad.question: Which boundaries are produced by an arrangement, and which confront it as material resistance?

sol-lewitt__judith-butler.text: Sol LeWitt's instructions can persist as works only by being executed again and again. Judith Butler likewise describes norms not as rigid things but as orders that remain effective through repeated enactments; performativity is not to be equated with a single performance. With LeWitt, the rule remains recognisable even though each realisation takes place in a different location, by different hands and under different conditions. With Butler, repetition produces social legibility and at the same time opens up possibilities of displacement. A particular time of the rule thus becomes visible: it seems to precede the individual enactment and yet can persist only by being enacted anew.
sol-lewitt__judith-butler.question: Can a rule really exist before its executions if it remains effective only through its repetition?

sol-lewitt__gilbert-simondon.text: Sol LeWitt's instruction remains recognisable even though each execution can become concrete in a different place. With transduction, Gilbert Simondon describes processes in which a structure does not simply copy itself but continues step by step under local conditions. LeWitt's rule travels through wall, material, scale and executing person. Its identity shows itself precisely in its ability to bring forth different realisations.
sol-lewitt__gilbert-simondon.question: How does a rule travel through different materials?

sol-lewitt__n-katherine-hayles.text: Sol LeWitt's work seems to make possible a radical separation of information and material carrier: an instruction can be stored, transmitted and executed anew on different walls. N. Katherine Hayles, however, draws attention to the fact that information never appears without some embodiment. LeWitt's rule, too, must be written, read, understood and materially realised. The wall is therefore not merely an interchangeable surface; it changes scale, bodily relation and perception.
sol-lewitt__n-katherine-hayles.question: What actually remains invariant when the same information takes on a different body?

roman-opalka__elena-esposito.text: Roman Opalka organises his work as a continuous sequence of numbers whose next step is formally predictable. Elena Esposito, by contrast, examines a future that remains future precisely because it cannot be fully known. Opalka's procedure brings the two into clear tension. Which number comes next is certain; whether and when it can actually be painted is not. The order knows its continuation; the body does not know its future.
roman-opalka__elena-esposito.question: How predictable is a future that has not yet arrived?

roman-opalka__heinz-von-foerster.text: Roman Opalka's next number arises from the preceding one and in turn becomes the precondition of the next. Heinz von Foerster's thinking of recursion describes exactly such operations, whose results re-enter the process. Yet Opalka's recursion has a peculiarity: it cannot return to its starting point. Each step extends the series and at the same time uses up lifetime. Recursion thereby becomes irreversible.
roman-opalka__heinz-von-foerster.question: What does recurrence mean when there is no return?

roman-opalka__michel-serres.text: Roman Opalka seems to construct a passage from one number to the next that is as free of interference as possible. Michel Serres is interested precisely in what intervenes in a passage: noise, deviation, parasite. With Opalka, this in-between sits in the body itself. Fatigue, voice, hand, age and finally death interrupt a sequence that could mathematically be continued without limit. The interference does not come to the system from outside; it belongs to its material execution.
roman-opalka__michel-serres.question: Does finitude first give an order its history?

roman-opalka__n-katherine-hayles.text: Roman Opalka's numbers can easily be noted as abstract information and continued digitally almost without limit. His work, however, does something else: the sequence is bound to a particular body, a hand, a voice and a lifetime. N. Katherine Hayles' critique of disembodied information therefore touches a sensitive point. The numbers can change body; the work cannot do so without further ado.
roman-opalka__n-katherine-hayles.question: When does the identity of a work end if its embodiment changes?

roman-opalka__susan-leigh-star.text: Susan Leigh Star examines classifications and infrastructures through which things receive stable places and different activities become coordinable. Roman Opalka's sequence of numbers seems to be the most unambiguous classification conceivable: each number has exactly one position. Yet the work binds this abstract order to a finite act of execution. Between two unambiguously determined places there suddenly lies something that no classification can fully absorb: lifetime spent.
roman-opalka__susan-leigh-star.question: What disappears from an order when it can give every event an unambiguous place?

christian-marclay__lucy-suchman.text: In The Clock, Christian Marclay assembles countless already produced film scenes into a temporal order that meets the actual time only in each particular screening. Lucy Suchman distinguishes between plans and situated action: an order can prepare action but cannot fully anticipate what happens in a concrete situation. Marclay's montage is fixed down to the last detail, yet its relation to the present arises anew every time. 16:23 is prepared in the film; that someone actually sits in front of it at 16:23 is an event. The structure organises the possibility of a coincidence without being able to store its experience.
christian-marclay__lucy-suchman.question: How much of an event can be prepared before it ceases to be an event?

christian-marclay__michel-foucault.text: Christian Marclay reorders a vast film archive according to a single property: the time of day shown. Michel Foucault is interested in the fact that archives do not simply preserve the past but establish orders under which something becomes findable and sayable. Marclay's montage suddenly turns completely different films into adjacent moments. Plot, genre and year of production recede; 14:01 follows 14:00. A new order thereby produces relations that were not present in the original material.
christian-marclay__michel-foucault.question: What history does a new order of the archive produce?

christian-marclay__michel-serres.text: Michel Serres is interested in transmission, passage and the interferences that arise in them. Christian Marclay works precisely with such transitions: a film cut connects spaces, times and stories that originally had nothing to do with one another. In The Clock, the transition must at the same time produce a strict temporal continuity. The cut separates and connects in the same moment. What is filmically discontinuous can thereby be experienced as a continuous present.
christian-marclay__michel-serres.question: Does continuity arise between events, or only through the operation that connects them?

christian-marclay__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.text: Christian Marclay produces a present out of already recorded images; Wendy Hui Kyong Chun examines digital presence as the effect of permanent updating. Both thereby call into question the supposed self-evidence of the „now“. With Marclay, the now consists of fragments of past films. In digital media, it arises from stored data, earlier behaviour and ever new updates. The present would then be less the opposite of storage than a particular way of actualising what is stored anew.
christian-marclay__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.question: How much past does a system need in order to be able to show us something as present?

bruce-nauman__elena-esposito.text: Bruce Nauman places bodies, language and actions in loops, repetitions and confined situations. Elena Esposito examines systems that generate expectations about an unknown future from past data. A loop seems at first to be the counter-model to prognosis: instead of opening up the future, it repeats the past. Yet every repetition at the same time generates an expectation of what is about to happen. The longer the repetition lasts, the more predictable the next repetition can become, and the more conspicuous a deviation would appear.
bruce-nauman__elena-esposito.question: When does repetition become a prognosis?

bruce-nauman__gilles-deleuze.text: Bruce Nauman repeats movements, gestures and sentences until their apparent identity becomes unstable. Gilles Deleuze disputes that repetition simply brings back the same. Nauman's body provides a difficult touchstone for this: an instruction can stay the same, but fatigue, attention and movement change. The repetition produces its difference partly through its own execution. Yet without a recognisable action, this change could not be observed as a difference of the same repetition.
bruce-nauman__gilles-deleuze.question: Does difference arise despite repetition, or precisely because something remains recognisable as repetition?

bruce-nauman__niklas-luhmann.text: Niklas Luhmann describes operations as events that vanish again in the very moment of their execution. Bruce Nauman can technically bring back the same movement as a video loop, seemingly without end. Two different times thus meet. The recording returns; the perceptual event of watching it does not. A technically identical state produces a sequence of non-identical presents.
bruce-nauman__niklas-luhmann.question: What actually repeats in a loop if the perception of its repetition can never return?

robert-smithson__michel-foucault.text: Michel Foucault examines institutions, archives and spatial arrangements in terms of how they distribute things, statements and visibilities to particular places. Robert Smithson's Site/Non-Site works bring a distant place into such an order through material, map, container and exhibition. The gallery therefore does not simply show the place; it dismantles, addresses and reorganises it under its own conditions. At the same time, the site persists outside the exhibition space and eludes its complete ordering. Smithson thereby makes visible that spatialisation means not only giving things a place but also determining under which order this place becomes observable.
robert-smithson__michel-foucault.question: What happens to a place when an institution reorders it?

robert-smithson__henri-bergson.text: Henri Bergson criticises a conception of time that treats change like a series of states lying spatially side by side. Robert Smithson, by contrast, works with actual space and at the same time with entropy, that is, with changes that cannot simply be reversed. Spiral Jetty remains spatially locatable and yet changes with water level, salt, material and time. The place remains findable without guaranteeing an identical state.
robert-smithson__henri-bergson.question: What does it mean to return to the same place when the place itself has taken on time?

robert-smithson__karen-barad.text: Karen Barad makes the apparatus a component of what becomes determinable through an observation. Robert Smithson's Site/Non-Site likewise does not separate cleanly between object and representation: material, map, gallery and distant place refer to one another reciprocally. The exhibition space does not simply show the place but produces a particular possibility of observing it. Nevertheless, the distant place remains outside this arrangement and has a history that the museum does not control.
robert-smithson__karen-barad.question: Where does an apparatus end when what it makes observable continues to happen spatially outside it?

robert-smithson__lucy-suchman.text: Lucy Suchman stresses that situations are not fully determined by preceding plans. Robert Smithson's interest in entropy confronts spatial planning with a similar limit. A form can be laid out, but material, weather and landscape continue their history. In Spiral Jetty, natural forces change the work continuously. The artistic decision thus produces not a completed form but the conditions of a further history.
robert-smithson__lucy-suchman.question: When does the execution of a plan end if its materials go on acting after the execution?

james-turrell__donna-haraway.text: James Turrell controls light and architecture so precisely that perception itself can become conspicuous. Donna Haraway insists that there is no view from nowhere. Turrell makes this situatedness bodily experienceable: even a different position, adaptation or lighting situation changes what can be seen. Perception thus has a place and a history. Yet the installation at the same time attempts to bring very different bodies into a common situation of perception.
james-turrell__donna-haraway.question: How common can a perception be if every gaze proceeds from a different bodily place?
